title: In 32 Allen Neuropixels mice, higher visual areas had steeper response spectra for natural scenes, gratings and movies; RF matching and RF-based model twins did not explain most of it
abstract: A source study found that cross-validated PCA spectra of natural-image responses decay faster (larger alpha) in areas higher in the anatomical mouse visual hierarchy. We tested whether this is specific to one stimulus set and whether receptive-field (RF) size and position explain it. We used all 32 Allen Visual Coding Neuropixels brain_observatory_1.1 mice (11,559 units in LGd, LP and six cortical areas) and a plan with decision rules written before the analysis. The hierarchy slope of alpha (ranks 2-30, 300-unit populations) was positive for natural scenes (0.27; 95% half-sample interval 0.19 to 0.34), static gratings (0.91; 0.78 to 1.04), natural movie one (0.45; 0.36 to 0.54) and natural movie three (0.35; 0.23 to 0.47), and inside cortex for all four sets. Matching RF area and RF position across cortical areas (99 units per area) did not lower the slope (natural scenes 0.21 matched, 0.23 unmatched; difference -0.02, interval -0.32 to 0.29), but this test has low power. Image-computable model twins with the measured RF centre, size, spatial frequency, orientation and simple/complex class of each unit gave slopes of 0.09 to 0.11 with equal weights against 0.27 in the data, and 49% to 69% of the data slope with reliability weights at generous RF sizes. Exploratory: the phase-invariant share of grating variance increased along the hierarchy, and the phase-dependent part had no cortical trend. Limitations: area-level correlational tests over 6 to 8 areas, a selected RF-defined subset, a simple uncalibrated twin model, and half-sample intervals that replaced a biased planned bootstrap. Code, aggregate results and exact provenance are included; Allen data stay external.
